title: Reduce alert fatigue via dynamic suppression windows and signature-based deduplication
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's oncall teams are receiving a high volume of burn-rate and latency alerts during noisy bursts that are operationally uninteresting (e.g., transient infra GC spikes, maintenance windows, traffic spikes from partner jobs). This results in alert fatigue and increases mean time to acknowledge for real incidents. Existing measures (static suppression windows and simple dedup keys) are insufficient for: multi-service cascades, noisy upstream flapping, and alerts with slight metric-value variation across multiple routes.

Goal:
Design and implement an adaptive alert suppression and deduplication layer for SLO/burn-rate alerts that: (1) reduces duplicate pages for the same underlying fault, (2) preserves signal for true incidents (no suppression on confirmed anomalies), and (3) enables easy tuning by SREs/product owners per-service. Success metrics: 35-50% reduction in duplicate pages for the top-20 noisy SLOs, no more than 5% regression in time-to-detect for incidents (measured by first-alert-to-incident-open), and positive oncall feedback in postmortems for two consecutive cycles.

Design overview:
- Alert signature generation: compute a compact fingerprint for an alert using the tuple {service, SLO-id, dominant_error_type, top-3 affected hosts/regions, correlated trace-id sample}. Signatures are hashed and used to deduplicate pages within a sliding suppression window.
- Sliding suppression windows: suppression duration is adaptive based on historical recurrence of the signature. Fresh signatures (never seen before) get minimal suppression (30s), frequently recurring signatures get longer suppression (up to 30m).
- Burst mode and short-circuiting: when anomaly-detector flags the metric as a system-level anomaly (high-confidence), suppression is reduced/disabled to ensure visibility for broad incidents. Conversely, when anomaly-detector indicates noise (low-confidence), suppression can be increased.
- Dedup scope and routing: deduplication is scoped first to team-owned routing groups, with a fallback to org-wide scope for cross-service blast radius indicators. The routing layer will attach the canonical "fingerprint" to alert events so downstream oncall tooling can reconcile duplicates.
- Paging policies: implement a policy engine rule that prevents immediate paging for duplicate signatures if last page is unacknowledged within a grace window; instead, send a consolidated summary to Slack and update a dedicated dashboard panel with the aggregated fingerprint timeline.

Implementation plan:
1) Prototype signature generator as a small Go service (or library) consumed by alerting pipeline. Wire it into the existing tracing hook to sample a correlated trace-id. (Owner: Liam)
2) Extend alert pipeline (Kafka -> alert-router) to compute signatures and maintain a lightweight in-memory LRU store for recent signatures; implement adaptive suppression controller backed by Dynamo for persistence across replicas. (Owner: Eng Observability)
3) Integrate with anomaly-detection pipeline (ENG-23114) to fetch high-confidence anomaly flags via a shared Redis channel; define TTLs and degrade gracefully if detection service is unavailable. (Owner: Observability/ML infra)
4) Update paging policy rules in Ops Dispatcher to read signature metadata and enforce dedup/pause logic. Add opt-outs and tagging for critical alerts that must bypass suppression. (Owner: SRE)
5) Dashboard and post-facto analytics: add a new "Debounced Alerts" dashboard in Console showing signatures, suppression counts, and time-to-detect comparisons for affected SLOs. (Owner: Console team)
6) Staged rollout: alpha (internal SRE), beta (selected services), GA (org-wide). Monitor key metrics and run weekly oncall reviews during beta.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Accuracy vs latency: richer signatures (more dimensions) reduce false dedups but increase compute/serialization cost and may prevent grouping the same incident across variants. We will iterate: start conservative (few dimensions) and increase as we observe false merges.
- State storage: in-memory LRU is fast but loses state on restart; persistent store (Dynamo) adds complexity and cost. A hybrid approach with in-memory and async persistence was chosen to keep page latency low.
- Anomaly detector coupling: relying on the ML detector improves decisions but creates a dependency. Mitigation: fall back to heuristics when detector is unavailable.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for signature collision probability (fuzz tests) and suppression window behavior.
- Integration tests simulating multi-service cascades and verifying dedup behavior across replicas.
- Canary in staging with synthetic bursts (k6-based traffic) to measure duplicate page rates, TTD, and any missed incidents.
- Runbook updates and oncall training session scheduled before beta rollout.

Review notes and approvals:
- 2026-02-20: Draft design reviewed with SRE and Console leads; action: add opt-out tag for urgent alerting (done).
- 2026-02-25: Security reviewed mitigations around including trace-id sample in signature; agreed to hash trace-id and keep only first 8 bytes.
- 2026-03-02: Performance review requested for in-memory LRU memory budget; Ops asked for a config flag to cap entries per service (in progress).

Blockers:
- Need a stable anomaly-detector contract from ENG-23114 team; currently in progress.
- Final quota approvals for Dynamo write capacity for persistence (ticket sent to infra finance).
